request.job_description: We are hiring an Engineering Manager to lead a team of 6-8 software engineers building our core B2B platform. The manager is responsible for delivery planning, hiring and onboarding, performance management and coaching, cross-functional collaboration with product and design, and maintaining engineering quality and team health. Candidates should have experience managing engineers, handling underperformance, and communicating clearly with stakeholders.

transcript.question: Tell me about how you develop the engineers on your team. Can you give a specific example of someone you helped grow?
transcript.answer: I think development is really important. I try to have regular one on ones and give people feedback. I encourage them to learn new things and take on challenges. Everyone on my team has grown a lot, I would say, because I support them and make sure they have what they need.

transcript.question: Walk me through a project you delivered that was at risk of slipping. What did you do?
transcript.answer: We had a few projects where timelines were tight. I made sure everyone was aligned and we worked hard to get it done. Sometimes you just have to push the team a bit and remind them of the deadline. In the end it shipped, more or less on time, I think. Agile helps with this a lot.

transcript.question: Describe a time you managed an engineer who was underperforming.
transcript.answer: I haven't had many of those honestly. If someone isn't performing, I think the best approach is to just let them figure it out and not micromanage. If it keeps up then you'd probably have to let HR handle it. I had one person who left on their own eventually so it worked out.

transcript.question: Two of your senior engineers disagree strongly about a technical approach and it's blocking the team. How do you handle it?
transcript.answer: I would probably just make the decision myself so we can move forward. Someone has to be the boss. I'd pick the approach that seems best and tell them to commit. Usually people get over it.

transcript.question: How do you communicate bad news, like a delay, to product or other stakeholders?
transcript.answer: I try to be transparent. I would tell them there is a delay and explain that engineering is complicated and estimates are just estimates. I usually do that in a meeting or Slack, whichever is easier. They generally understand.
